confucius.name: Confucius
confucius.summary: Kong Qiu, known in the West as Confucius, was a teacher and minor official from the state of Lu in China's Spring and Autumn period. His sayings, gathered by his followers in the Analects, became the heart of the Confucian tradition, with its care for humaneness, ritual propriety and learning.

hillel-the-elder.name: Hillel the Elder
hillel-the-elder.dates: fl. late 1st century BCE – early 1st century CE
hillel-the-elder.summary: Hillel was a Jewish sage, born in Babylonia, who taught in Jerusalem around the turn of the Common Era. His sayings are preserved in the Mishnah and the Talmud, and the school that followed him, the House of Hillel, shaped much of later Jewish law.

jesus.name: Jesus
jesus.summary: Jesus of Nazareth was a Jewish preacher and teacher in Galilee and Judea under Roman rule. His teaching is preserved in the Gospels of the New Testament, written in the decades after his death; Christians revere him as the Christ and the Son of God.

the-buddha.name: The Buddha
the-buddha.summary: Siddhartha Gautama, called the Buddha, 'the awakened one', was a wandering teacher in north-eastern India whose teaching became the foundation of Buddhism. His discourses were handed down orally by the monastic community and later written down, most fully in the Pali Canon.

alan-watts.name: Alan Watts
alan-watts.summary: Alan Watts was a British-born writer and speaker who spent most of his adult life in the United States. Through books such as The Way of Zen (1957) and many recorded talks, he introduced Zen, Taoism and other Asian philosophies to a wide Western audience.

marcus-aurelius.name: Marcus Aurelius
marcus-aurelius.summary: Marcus Aurelius was Roman emperor from 161 to 180 CE and a lifelong student of Stoic philosophy. The private notes he wrote to himself, known as the Meditations, are among the most widely read works of Stoicism.

jordan-peterson.name: Jordan B. Peterson
jordan-peterson.summary: Jordan B. Peterson is a Canadian clinical psychologist and professor emeritus of psychology at the University of Toronto. His self-help book 12 Rules for Life (2018) became an international bestseller.

albert-camus.name: Albert Camus
albert-camus.summary: Albert Camus was a French writer and philosopher, born in Algeria, whose novels and essays explore what he called the absurd: our longing for meaning in a world that offers none. His works include The Stranger (1942) and The Myth of Sisyphus (1942), and he received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1957.

robert-baden-powell.name: Robert Baden-Powell
robert-baden-powell.summary: Robert Baden-Powell was a British Army officer who founded the Scout movement; his handbook Scouting for Boys appeared in 1908. He served as Chief Scout of the World until his death in Kenya in 1941.

kelly-johnson.name: Kelly Johnson
kelly-johnson.summary: Clarence 'Kelly' Johnson was an American aeronautical engineer who led Lockheed's Skunk Works, where aircraft such as the U-2 and SR-71 were designed. The design rule 'keep it simple, stupid' is commonly credited to him, though the attribution rests on later accounts.

joseph-juran.name: Joseph M. Juran
joseph-juran.summary: Joseph M. Juran was a Romanian-born American engineer and management consultant, known for his work on quality management. He popularised the idea of 'the vital few and the trivial many' and named it the Pareto principle, after the economist Vilfredo Pareto.

laurence-j-peter.name: Laurence J. Peter
laurence-j-peter.summary: Laurence J. Peter was a Canadian-born educator and writer. With Raymond Hull he wrote The Peter Principle (1969), which argues that people in a hierarchy tend to rise to their 'level of incompetence'.

popular-saying.name: Popular saying
popular-saying.summary: Sayings that pass from person to person, in print and online, without a known author. We include them because many people live by them, label them honestly, and keep looking for where they came from.

torah-writers.name: Authors of the Torah
torah-writers.dates: compiled over centuries; final form c. 5th century BCE (scholarly estimate)
torah-writers.summary: The Torah, the first five books of the Hebrew Bible, is traditionally attributed to Moses. Most modern scholars see it as the work of several writers and editors whose material was brought together over centuries, reaching its final form around the Persian period.
torah-writers.label: Scripture

qoheleth.name: Qoheleth (the Preacher)
qoheleth.summary: Qoheleth, a Hebrew title usually rendered 'the Preacher' or 'the Teacher', is the voice that speaks in the book of Ecclesiastes. Jewish and Christian tradition identified him with King Solomon; most modern scholars regard the author as unknown and date the book to between the mid-5th and early 2nd centuries BCE.

hebrew-wisdom-writers.name: Hebrew wisdom writers
hebrew-wisdom-writers.dates: collected over several centuries; final form c. 5th–4th century BCE (scholarly estimate)
hebrew-wisdom-writers.summary: The sayings of the Book of Proverbs are traditionally attributed to King Solomon, and the book itself also names other sages, such as Agur and Lemuel. Scholars see it as a collection of Israelite wisdom gathered over several centuries, probably reaching its final form in the Persian or early Hellenistic period.
hebrew-wisdom-writers.label: Scripture

paul-the-apostle.name: Paul the Apostle
paul-the-apostle.summary: Paul of Tarsus was a Jew who joined the early followers of Jesus and became their most influential missionary to non-Jews. Thirteen New Testament letters bear his name: scholars widely accept seven as his own, while others, such as Ephesians, Colossians and the letters to Timothy, are traditionally attributed to him but disputed.

rene-descartes.name: René Descartes
rene-descartes.summary: René Descartes was a French philosopher, mathematician and scientist, often called the father of modern philosophy. His Discourse on the Method (1637) sets out a way of reasoning from doubt to certainty, beginning from 'I think, therefore I am'.

henry-david-thoreau.name: Henry David Thoreau
henry-david-thoreau.summary: Henry David Thoreau was an American essayist, naturalist and a leading voice of New England Transcendentalism. Walden (1854) reflects on the two years he spent living simply in a cabin by Walden Pond, and his essay on civil disobedience has inspired movements of nonviolent resistance.

aristotle.name: Aristotle
aristotle.summary: Aristotle was a Greek philosopher, a student of Plato and tutor to Alexander the Great, who founded his own school, the Lyceum, in Athens. His works range across logic, science, politics and ethics; the Nicomachean Ethics explores virtue as a settled habit and a mean between extremes.

carol-dweck.name: Carol S. Dweck
carol-dweck.summary: Carol S. Dweck is an American psychologist and professor at Stanford University. Her research on 'fixed' and 'growth' mindsets reached a wide audience through her book Mindset (2006).

barry-schwartz.name: Barry Schwartz
barry-schwartz.summary: Barry Schwartz is an American psychologist who taught for many years at Swarthmore College. In The Paradox of Choice (2004) he argues that having too many options can leave people less satisfied.

buddhist-monastic-routine.name: Buddhist monastic routine (popular summary)
buddhist-monastic-routine.summary: A present-day popular summary of the daily rhythm kept in Buddhist monasteries, noted from a video in the project's seed notes. It has not yet been checked against the monastic code (Vinaya) or any other Buddhist text, so it is shown as unverified.

author-of-job.name: Author of the Book of Job
author-of-job.summary: The Book of Job, a poetic meditation on suffering and justice, does not name its author. A tradition recorded in the Talmud credits it to Moses; modern scholars regard the author as unknown and generally date the book to between the 6th and 4th centuries BCE.

krishna.name: Krishna
krishna.summary: Krishna is revered in Hinduism as a deity, an avatar of Vishnu and, in many traditions, the Supreme Being. In the Bhagavad Gita, part of the epic Mahabharata, he speaks as charioteer and teacher to the warrior Arjuna on the eve of battle.

epictetus.name: Epictetus
epictetus.summary: Epictetus was a Greek Stoic philosopher, born a slave in Hierapolis in Phrygia, who taught in Rome and later at Nicopolis in Greece. He wrote nothing himself; his student Arrian recorded his teaching in the Discourses and the short handbook known as the Enchiridion.

laozi.name: Laozi
laozi.summary: Laozi, 'the Old Master', is the sage traditionally credited with the Tao Te Ching and honoured as the founder of Taoism. The earliest account of his life, by the historian Sima Qian around 100 BCE, already mixes legend with history, and many scholars think the text grew from more than one hand.

muhammad.name: The Prophet Muhammad
muhammad.summary: Muhammad, born in Mecca, is revered by Muslims as the final prophet of God, to whom the Qur'an was revealed. Reports of his words and deeds (hadith) were passed on by his companions and later gathered into collections such as Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim.

quran.name: The Qur'an
quran.dates: revealed c. 610–632 CE; standard text compiled c. 650 CE
quran.summary: The Qur'an is the central scripture of Islam, believed by Muslims to be the word of God revealed to the Prophet Muhammad over some twenty-three years. According to Islamic tradition, its standard written text was compiled under the caliph Uthman around 650 CE.

socrates.name: Socrates
socrates.summary: Socrates was an Athenian philosopher who wrote nothing himself and is known mainly through the dialogues of his student Plato and the writings of Xenophon. He was tried and executed in Athens in 399 BCE; how closely Plato's Socrates matches the historical man is still debated.

psalmists.name: The Psalmists
psalmists.dates: composed over several centuries, c. 10th–4th century BCE or later (scholarly estimate)
psalmists.summary: The Book of Psalms gathers 150 songs and prayers of ancient Israel. Many carry headings naming David, and Psalm 90 is headed 'a prayer of Moses'; scholars see the collection as the work of many poets over several centuries, gathered for worship.
psalmists.label: Scripture

homer.name: Homer
homer.summary: Homer is the poet traditionally credited with the Iliad and the Odyssey, the oldest surviving works of Greek literature. The ancient Greeks treated him as a real person, but modern scholars debate whether he existed and how the epics, rooted in oral tradition, came to be written down.

alexander-pope.name: Alexander Pope
alexander-pope.summary: Alexander Pope was an English poet of the Augustan age, known for his satire and his translations of Homer. An Essay on Criticism, begun in his late teens and published in 1711 when he was in his early twenties, gave English many lasting phrases, among them 'to err is human, to forgive divine'.

heraclitus.name: Heraclitus
heraclitus.summary: Heraclitus of Ephesus was a Greek philosopher who taught that the world is always changing, held together by an underlying order he called the logos. His book is lost and survives only in fragments quoted by later writers such as Plutarch and Clement of Alexandria.

author-of-joshua.name: Author of the Book of Joshua
author-of-joshua.summary: The Book of Joshua tells of Israel's entry into Canaan under Joshua, Moses' successor. Jewish tradition attributed it to Joshua himself; most modern scholars see it as part of a longer history composed and edited around the 7th and 6th centuries BCE.

james.name: James
james.summary: The Letter of James opens in the name of 'James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ'. Tradition identifies him with James the brother of Jesus, a leader of the church in Jerusalem who died around 62 CE; many modern scholars think the letter was written later in his name.

zechariah.name: Zechariah
zechariah.summary: Zechariah was a Hebrew prophet in Jerusalem after the return from exile in Babylon, who encouraged the rebuilding of the Temple. Scholars generally credit him with chapters 1–8 of the book that bears his name and attribute chapters 9–14 to later writers.
zechariah.label: Scripture

author-of-hebrews.name: Author of Hebrews
author-of-hebrews.summary: The Epistle to the Hebrews is an early Christian sermon in letter form that does not name its author. It was long attributed to Paul, but its author is unknown; it was probably written in the second half of the 1st century CE.

zeno-of-citium.name: Zeno of Citium
zeno-of-citium.summary: Zeno of Citium, from Cyprus, founded the Stoic school in Athens around 300 BCE, teaching at the Stoa Poikile, the Painted Porch that gave Stoicism its name. His writings are lost except for fragments; his sayings are known through later authors such as Diogenes Laertius.

micah.name: Micah
micah.summary: Micah of Moresheth was a Hebrew prophet in Judah in the late 8th century BCE, a contemporary of Isaiah. The book that bears his name speaks out against injustice and is best known for its summary of what God asks: to do justly, love mercy and walk humbly.
micah.label: Scripture

hippocrates.name: Hippocrates
hippocrates.summary: Hippocrates of Kos was a Greek physician, often called the father of medicine. The Hippocratic Corpus, some sixty early medical writings, bears his name, though scholars think most were written by different authors of his school.

mahavira.name: Mahavira
mahavira.dates: traditionally 599–527 BCE; many scholars place him in the 5th century BCE
mahavira.summary: Mahavira, born Vardhamana, is revered in Jainism as the twenty-fourth and last tirthankara of the present age. A contemporary of the Buddha, he taught non-violence (ahimsa) and self-discipline, and his teachings were passed on by his disciples in the Jain scriptures.

blaise-pascal.name: Blaise Pascal
blaise-pascal.summary: Blaise Pascal was a French mathematician, physicist and Christian thinker. His Pensées ('Thoughts'), notes towards a defence of Christianity left unfinished at his death, were published in 1670.

benjamin-franklin.name: Benjamin Franklin
benjamin-franklin.summary: Benjamin Franklin was an American printer, writer, scientist and statesman, one of the Founding Fathers of the United States. His Autobiography, begun in 1771 and left unfinished, describes his plan for practising thirteen virtues.

talmudic-sages.name: Rabbis of the Talmud
talmudic-sages.summary: The Babylonian Talmud records the debates, teachings and stories of generations of rabbis, building on the Mishnah. Many of its lessons come as stories, like that of Honi the Circle-Drawer and the man planting a carob tree.

leonardo-da-vinci.name: Leonardo da Vinci
leonardo-da-vinci.summary: Leonardo da Vinci was an Italian painter, engineer and scientist of the Renaissance, whose notebooks record his studies of nature, anatomy and machines. The saying 'Simplicity is the ultimate sophistication' is often credited to him, but no source for it in his writings has been found.

king-tang.name: Tang of Shang
king-tang.summary: Tang was the founding king of the Shang dynasty in ancient China, traditionally dated to around 1600 BCE, and is honoured in the Confucian classics as a model ruler. The Great Learning quotes a motto said to have been inscribed on his bathing tub; the inscription is known only through this much later text.

oliver-goldsmith.name: Oliver Goldsmith
oliver-goldsmith.summary: Oliver Goldsmith was an Irish novelist, playwright and poet, author of The Vicar of Wakefield and She Stoops to Conquer. The Citizen of the World (1762) gathers his letters written in the voice of a fictional Chinese philosopher visiting London.

plato.name: Plato
plato.summary: Plato was an Athenian philosopher, a student of Socrates and the teacher of Aristotle, who founded the Academy in Athens. Most of his works are dialogues in which Socrates is the main speaker, among them the Apology, the Gorgias and the Cratylus.

diogenes-laertius.name: Diogenes Laertius
diogenes-laertius.summary: Diogenes Laertius was a biographer of the Greek philosophers about whose own life almost nothing is known. His Lives of Eminent Philosophers, probably written in the first half of the 3rd century CE, preserves many sayings and anecdotes found nowhere else.

will-durant.name: Will Durant
will-durant.summary: Will Durant was an American historian and writer who brought philosophy and history to a wide readership. The Story of Philosophy (1926) became a bestseller, and he went on to write the eleven-volume Story of Civilization, the last five volumes jointly with his wife Ariel. The line 'We are what we repeatedly do' comes from his summary of Aristotle and is often quoted as Aristotle's own.

aleksandr-solzhenitsyn.name: Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn
aleksandr-solzhenitsyn.summary: Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn was a Russian novelist and historian. Arrested in 1945 while serving as a Red Army officer for criticising Stalin in private letters, he spent eight years in labour camps and later wrote about them in One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich (1962) and The Gulag Archipelago. He received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1970, was expelled from the Soviet Union in 1974, and returned to Russia in 1994.

fyodor-dostoevsky.name: Fyodor Dostoevsky
fyodor-dostoevsky.summary: Fyodor Dostoevsky was a Russian novelist whose books probe faith, doubt, guilt and freedom. Arrested in 1849 for belonging to a radical circle, he faced a mock execution and spent four years in a Siberian prison camp. His major novels include Crime and Punishment (1866), The Idiot, Demons and The Brothers Karamazov (1879–80).

michel-de-montaigne.name: Michel de Montaigne
michel-de-montaigne.summary: Michel de Montaigne was a French writer of the Renaissance who, after retiring to his estate near Bordeaux, began writing short, searching pieces about himself and human nature. He called them essais, 'attempts', and so gave the essay its name; they were first published in 1580 and expanded in 1588. He also served as mayor of Bordeaux.

baruch-spinoza.name: Baruch Spinoza
baruch-spinoza.summary: Baruch (Benedictus de) Spinoza was a Dutch philosopher of Portuguese-Jewish descent, born in Amsterdam. Expelled from the city's Jewish community in 1656, he earned a modest living grinding lenses and wrote works that shaped modern philosophy, among them the Ethics, published after his death in 1677.

immanuel-kant.name: Immanuel Kant
immanuel-kant.summary: Immanuel Kant was a German philosopher of the Enlightenment who lived and taught in Königsberg, Prussia, all his life. His Critique of Pure Reason (1781) and his moral philosophy, built on the 'categorical imperative' set out in the Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals (1785), are among the most influential works in Western thought.

arthur-schopenhauer.name: Arthur Schopenhauer
arthur-schopenhauer.summary: Arthur Schopenhauer was a German philosopher, born in Danzig, known for the pessimism of his main work, The World as Will and Representation (1818/1819). He was among the first Western philosophers to draw on Indian thought, and he found a wide readership late in life with the essays of Parerga and Paralipomena (1851).

friedrich-nietzsche.name: Friedrich Nietzsche
friedrich-nietzsche.summary: Friedrich Nietzsche was a German philosopher and classical scholar who became a professor at Basel at the age of 24. In books such as Thus Spoke Zarathustra and Twilight of the Idols he questioned inherited morality and religion and asked how life can be affirmed. A collapse in January 1889 ended his working life.

soren-kierkegaard.name: Søren Kierkegaard
soren-kierkegaard.summary: Søren Kierkegaard was a Danish philosopher and Christian thinker from Copenhagen, often called the first existentialist. Many of his books, such as Either/Or and Fear and Trembling (both 1843), appeared under pseudonyms, while religious works like Works of Love (1847) were signed with his own name.

joseph-campbell.name: Joseph Campbell
joseph-campbell.summary: Joseph Campbell was an American writer on comparative mythology and religion who taught literature at Sarah Lawrence College for 38 years. His book The Hero with a Thousand Faces (1949) set out the 'monomyth', a shared pattern of the hero's journey across the world's myths. His conversations with Bill Moyers, broadcast after his death as The Power of Myth (1988), made the phrase 'follow your bliss' widely known.

stephen-covey.name: Stephen R. Covey
stephen-covey.summary: Stephen R. Covey was an American educator, author and speaker, and a professor at Utah State University's Jon M. Huntsman School of Business at the time of his death. His best-known book is The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People (1989), and in 1996 Time magazine named him one of the 25 most influential people.

james-clear.name: James Clear
james-clear.summary: James Clear is an American writer, raised in Hamilton, Ohio, who writes about habits and decision-making. He is best known for Atomic Habits (2018), which argues that small, steady changes in behaviour add up to lasting change.

ryan-holiday.name: Ryan Holiday
ryan-holiday.summary: Ryan Holiday is an American author and marketer who has done much to bring Stoic philosophy, especially that of Marcus Aurelius, to a modern popular readership. His books include The Obstacle Is the Way (2014) and Ego Is the Enemy (2016).

mark-manson.name: Mark Manson
mark-manson.summary: Mark Manson is an American self-help author and blogger. His bestseller The Subtle Art of Not Giving a F*ck (2016) argues that life's struggles give it meaning and pushes back against relentless positive thinking.

brene-brown.name: Brené Brown
brene-brown.summary: Brené Brown is an American academic, author and podcaster who holds an endowed chair at the University of Houston's Graduate College of Social Work. She is known for her research on shame, vulnerability and courage, for her widely viewed 2010 TEDx talk 'The power of vulnerability', and for books such as Daring Greatly (2012).

viktor-frankl.name: Viktor E. Frankl
viktor-frankl.summary: Viktor Frankl was an Austrian neurologist and psychiatrist who survived the Nazi concentration camps. He founded logotherapy, a school of psychotherapy that sees the search for meaning as the central human motivation, and described his camp experiences in Man's Search for Meaning (1946).

eckhart-tolle.name: Eckhart Tolle
eckhart-tolle.summary: Eckhart Tolle, born Ulrich Leonard Tölle in Lünen, Germany, is a spiritual teacher and self-help author not tied to any particular religion. His books The Power of Now (1997) and A New Earth (2005) invite readers to rest their attention in the present moment.

naval-ravikant.name: Naval Ravikant
naval-ravikant.summary: Naval Ravikant is an Indian-born American entrepreneur and investor, co-founder and chairman of AngelList. He hosts his own podcast on philosophy, happiness and wealth, and has been a guest on The Joe Rogan Experience and The Tim Ferriss Show.

tim-ferriss.name: Tim Ferriss
tim-ferriss.summary: Tim Ferriss is an American entrepreneur, investor, author and podcaster, host of The Tim Ferriss Show. He is known for his 4-Hour series of books, beginning with The 4-Hour Workweek (2007), and for his exercise of 'fear-setting', which he draws from Stoic writers such as Seneca.

andrew-huberman.name: Andrew Huberman
andrew-huberman.summary: Andrew Huberman is an American neuroscientist and associate professor of neurobiology and ophthalmology at the Stanford University School of Medicine. Since 2021 he has hosted the widely heard Huberman Lab podcast on health and science; some scientists have criticised claims made on it as poorly evidenced.

jocko-willink.name: Jocko Willink
jocko-willink.summary: Jocko Willink is an American author, podcaster and retired U.S. Navy SEAL officer who served in the Iraq War. He co-wrote Extreme Ownership (2015) with Leif Babin, and after appearing on the podcasts of Tim Ferriss, Joe Rogan and Sam Harris he started the Jocko Podcast in 2015.

donald-knuth.name: Donald Knuth
donald-knuth.summary: Donald Knuth is an American computer scientist and mathematician, professor emeritus at Stanford University and recipient of the 1974 ACM Turing Award. He is the author of The Art of Computer Programming and has been called the father of the analysis of algorithms.

william-shakespeare.name: William Shakespeare
william-shakespeare.summary: William Shakespeare was an English playwright and poet, born in Stratford-upon-Avon and active in London. His plays, among them The Merchant of Venice, written in the 1590s, are among the most performed and quoted in the English language.

ptahhotep.name: Ptahhotep
ptahhotep.dates: set in the 5th Dynasty (c. 25th–24th century BCE); surviving copies date from the Middle Kingdom (c. 20th–19th century BCE)
ptahhotep.summary: Ptahhotep was a vizier of the Egyptian Old Kingdom to whom The Instruction of Ptahhotep, one of the oldest surviving works of wisdom literature, is credited. Most Egyptologists think the attribution is a literary device and that the text was written down later, in the Middle Kingdom.

ohiyesa.name: Ohiyesa (Charles A. Eastman)
ohiyesa.summary: Charles Alexander Eastman, born Ohiyesa, was a Santee Dakota physician, writer and reformer. Raised in the traditional Dakota way until about fifteen, he later trained in medicine at Boston University and wrote some of the first books by a Native American author about Native life. He had become a Christian, and his accounts of Dakota belief are written from that later vantage and sometimes speak of 'the Indian' in general.

upanishads.name: Upanishadic sages
upanishads.label: Scripture
upanishads.summary: The Upanishads are the late Vedic texts in which teachers and students explore the self, Brahman and right conduct. They were composed and handed down orally by many hands over centuries; the Brihadaranyaka and Taittiriya are among the oldest. Teachers named in them, such as Yajnavalkya, are known only from the texts themselves.

vyasa.name: Vyasa
vyasa.dates: traditional; the Mahabharata grew between about the 4th century BCE and the 4th century CE
vyasa.summary: Vyasa is the sage traditionally credited with composing the Mahabharata, in which he also appears as a character. Scholars see the epic as the work of many poets and editors over several centuries, so Vyasa stands for that tradition rather than a single datable author.

tiruvalluvar.name: Tiruvalluvar
tiruvalluvar.dates: variously dated between about the 1st century BCE and the 5th century CE
tiruvalluvar.summary: Tiruvalluvar is the poet traditionally credited with the Tirukkural, the classic Tamil book of 1,330 short couplets on virtue, wealth and love. Almost nothing reliable is known of his life, and both Jain and Hindu traditions have claimed him.

saadi.name: Saadi
saadi.summary: Saadi of Shiraz was a Persian poet and prose writer, one of the major figures of classical Persian literature. After years of travel he wrote the Bustan (1257) and the Gulistan (1258), collections of stories, verses and moral sayings that were long used to teach Persian across the Islamic world.

bahaullah.name: Bahá’u’lláh
bahaullah.summary: Bahá’u’lláh, born Mírzá Ḥusayn-ʻAlí Núrí in Tehran, founded the Bahá’í Faith. Exiled from Persia and imprisoned by the Ottoman authorities, he wrote extensively, and The Hidden Words, composed in Baghdad around 1858, is one of his best-known works.

avesta-authors.name: Authors of the Avesta
avesta-authors.label: Scripture
avesta-authors.dates: Younger Avestan texts, perhaps 6th–4th century BCE; written down much later
avesta-authors.summary: The Avesta is the body of Zoroastrian sacred texts. Apart from the Gathas ascribed to Zarathustra, its hymns, including the Yashts to individual divinities such as Mithra, were composed by generations of priests and handed down orally before being written down in the Sasanian period.

yoruba-proverbs.name: Yoruba proverbs
yoruba-proverbs.dates: oral tradition of uncertain age; the sayings here were recorded in 1894
yoruba-proverbs.summary: Proverbs (owe) are a central part of Yoruba speech and teaching in what is now south-western Nigeria, Benin and Togo. The sayings quoted here were collected and translated by the British colonial officer A. B. Ellis, so the English wording is his and the sayings are older than their recording.

akan-proverbs.name: Akan (Ashanti) proverbs
akan-proverbs.dates: oral tradition of uncertain age; collected in 1879 and translated in 1916
akan-proverbs.summary: Proverbs (ebe) carry much of the moral teaching of the Akan peoples of present-day Ghana, including the Asante (Ashanti). The sayings quoted here come from J. G. Christaller's 1879 Twi collection as translated and annotated by the colonial anthropologist R. S. Rattray in 1916.

mozi.name: Mozi
mozi.summary: Mozi (Mo Di) was a Chinese thinker of the Warring States period and founder of the Mohist school. Against the graded loyalties of the Confucians he argued for impartial care (jian ai) for all people, and against offensive war. The book that bears his name was compiled by his followers.

taishang-ganying-pian.name: Treatise on Action and Response
taishang-ganying-pian.summary: The Taishang Ganying Pian is an anonymous Daoist morality book that teaches that good and bad deeds bring due reward and punishment. It blends Daoist, Confucian and Buddhist ethics and became one of the most widely printed religious tracts in late imperial China.

zhuangzi.name: Zhuangzi
zhuangzi.summary: Zhuang Zhou, known as Zhuangzi, was a Chinese thinker of the Warring States period and, with Laozi, the main early voice of Taoism. The book named after him mixes stories, dialogues and jokes; scholars usually credit him with the Inner Chapters and see the rest, including the story of his wife's death, as the work of later followers.

prince-shotoku.name: Prince Shōtoku
prince-shotoku.summary: Prince Shōtoku was regent of Japan under Empress Suiko and a great patron of Buddhism. The Nihongi (720) credits him with the Seventeen-Article Constitution of 604, which draws on Confucian and Buddhist ideals; some historians doubt that he wrote it himself.
